FP-OFFICIAL MESSAGE-ENG
Dear San Joaquin County Voter,
Thank you for being a registered voter! Your participation in elections ensures that your voice is heard
in decisions affecting your community and day-to-day life, including proposed laws and local, state,
and national candidates.
This County Voter Information Guide is provided for your review to help you prepare for the Tuesday,
November 3, 2026, General Election. The included sample ballot may be used for practice to reduce
errors on your official ballot. All eligible registered voters will be mailed an official ballot no later than
October 5, 2026.
Additional details are available in the State Voter Information Guide, which will be mailed separately
and posted online at www.voterguide.sos.ca.gov
Candidate Statements: Statements are submitted voluntarily by candidates and printed at their
expense. They are not edited after submission. For a complete list of candidates, see the sample
ballot in this guide (Elections Code §13312(a)).
Congressional Boundary Changes for 2026: With the passage of Proposition 50, California adopted
new legislatively drawn U.S. House district maps for elections from 2026 through 2030. As a result,
some San Joaquin County voters will be assigned to different congressional districts in this election.
No Wrong Location: A countywide voting model that allows San Joaquin County voters to vote at
any polling place in the county, regardless of assigned precinct.
Sign, Scan, and Go: A streamlined in-person voting process that allows voters to check in quickly
and proceed directly to cast their pre-mailed vote-by-mail ballot.
Adopt-a-Poll: A community partnership program enabling businesses, organizations, or families to
sponsor and help staff polling locations. More information can be found at www.sjgov.org/adopt-a-poll
Text-to-Cure: A secure new process that allows voters to receive a text message notification and
resolve challenged signature issues online before the deadline.
For assistance, call (209) 468-VOTE (8683) or email registration@sjgov.org
Sincerely,
Olivia Hale
San Joaquin County Registrar of Voters
An Official Message From the
San Joaquin County Registrar of Voters

FP-VOTER BILL OF RIGHTS-ENG
VOTER BILL OF RIGHTS
1. The right to vote if you are a registered voter. You are eligible to vote if you are:
• a U.S. citizen living in California
• at least 18 years old
• registered where you currently live
• not currently serving a state or federal prison term for the conviction of a felony
• not currently found mentally incompetent to vote by a court
2. The right to vote if you are a registered voter even if your name is not on the
list. You will vote using a provisional ballot. Your vote will be counted if elections
officials determine that you are eligible to vote.
3. The right to vote if you are still in line when the polls close.
4. The right to cast a secret ballot without anyone bothering you or telling you how
to vote.
5. The right to get a new ballot if you have made a mistake, if you have not already
cast your ballot. You can:
• Ask an elections official at a polling place for a new ballot,
• Exchange your vote-by-mail ballot for a new one at an elections office, or at
your polling place, or
• Vote using a provisional ballot.
6. The right to get help casting your ballot from anyone you choose, except from your
employer or union representative.
7. The right to drop off your completed vote-by-mail ballot at any polling place in
California.
8. The right to get election materials in a language other than English if enough
people in your voting precinct speak that language.
9. The right to ask questions to elections officials about election procedures and
watch the election process. If the person you ask cannot answer your questions,
they must send you to the right person for an answer. If you are disruptive, they
can stop answering you.
10. The right to report any illegal or fraudulent election activity to an elections official or
the Secretary of State’s office.
If you believe you have been denied any of these rights, or you are aware of any
election fraud or misconduct, please call the Secretary of State’s confidential
toll-free Voter Hotline at (800) 345-VOTE (8683).

FP-ELECTION SECURITY-ENG
ELECTION SECURITY
In San Joaquin County we use the Verity Voting system,
developed by Hart InterCivic. The Verity Voting system is a
certified and widely used voting solution in California. The
Verity Voting system is designed to meet rigorous security
and accessibility standards. It supports multiple voting
methods, including in-person voting at polling locations, as
well as mail-in ballots. The system includes an independent
voting experience for individuals with disabilities.
The KNOWiNK Poll Pad is used to modernize and
streamline the voter check-in process at polling
locations. These electronic poll books have replaced
traditional paper poll books, reducing wait times and
improving the accuracy of voter records.
The Verity system has undergone extensive testing and certification by
the California Secretary of State’s Office of Voting Systems Technology
Assessment (OVSTA). These evaluations cover aspects such as security,
usability, and functionality. The KNOWiNK Poll Pad has been certified for
use in California and is employed across various counties to improve the
efficiency and reliability of elections.
The California Secretary of State’s Office oversees the certification process
to ensure that both systems meet the State’s stringent security and
functionality standards.
TRUSTED SOURCES OF INFORMATION
Official announcements, such as deadlines and voting locations, will
always come from the San Joaquin County Registrar of Voters Office or the
California Secretary of State’s Office. If you are unsure about any voting or
election information, contact the Registrar of Voters Office at 209-468-VOTE
(8683) to verify it.

FP-WAYS TO VOTE-ENG
WAYS TO VOTE
All registered voters in California are automatically mailed a ballot before each election.
Vote in Person
Early voting will be available at our office, located at 44 N San Joaquin St., Suite 350, Stockton, CA
95202, from October 5 through November 2, 2026. We will be open Monday through Friday from 8:00
a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and on Saturday, October 31, 2026, from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
You can vote in person on Election Day, November 3, 2026. Polling locations will be open from 7:00
a.m. to 8:00 p.m.
To verify your assigned polling location, refer to the back of this guide or visit our website at
www.sjcrov.org
Vote-by-Mail
• MARK YOUR BALLOT Instructions on how to fill out your ballot are included.
• SEAL & SIGN your envelope. Your signature will be compared to the one you have
on file. If more than one voter per household, make sure you are signing the correct
envelope.
• RETURN ON TIME Ballots must be postmarked or returned by 8 p.m. on Election
Day to be counted. Make sure your vote counts by mailing your ballot early or
returning it in person to a polling location, an official ballot drop box, or the Registrar
of Voters Office.
Sign, Scan & Go
Help us process ballots efficiently and keep the vote count moving swiftly by using Sign, Scan & Go
when returning your voted ballot in person to our office or any polling location.
• SIGN in with an Election Officer.
• SCAN your ballot at the ballot scanner.
• GO It’s that easy!
DRIVE-UP DEMOCRACY
Drive-up democracy is a voting method aimed at enhancing accessibility and convenience by allowing
voters to cast their ballots from their vehicles. On Election Day, this service is available at the County
Administration Building, located at 44 N San Joaquin St., Stockton, CA 95202, from 7:00 a.m. to
8:00 p.m. Voters can drive up, hand their ballot to an Election Officer, who will then place it into our
secured drop box.
Ensure that your ballot is MARKED and that your envelope is SEALED & SIGNED

FP-VOTER ASSISTANCE-ENG
INFORMATION FOR VOTERS WITH DISABILITIES
Voter assistance in San Joaquin County encompasses a range
of services and resources designed to help voters understand
their rights, navigate the voting process, and overcome any
barriers they might face when casting their ballot.
POLLING LOCATION ASSISTANCE
Language Assistance: San Joaquin County provides voting materials
and assistance in multiple languages to accommodate voters who are not
proficient in English. Bilingual election officers are available at many polling
locations.
Disability Assistance: Polling locations are equipped with accessible
voting machines and other aids to assist voters with disabilities. Election
officers are trained to help voters who need assistance marking their ballot.
REMOTE ACCESSIBLE VOTE-BY-MAIL (RAVBM)
This service allows voters with disabilities to receive their ballot
electronically, mark it using their assistive technology, and return it by mail,
at a drop box location, or drop off in person. Access your ballot by visiting
our website at www.sjgov.org/RAVBM, and entering your information
through a secure portal.
CURBSIDE VOTING
Voters who are unable to enter the polling location due to physical
disabilities can request curbside voting. A poll worker will bring a ballot
to the voter’s vehicle, assist as needed, and ensure the ballot is securely
returned.

유권자들은 1965년 투표권법(Voting Rights Act of 1965)에 따라 투표용지
및 기타 선거 자료를 스페인어로 제공받을 수 있습니다. 투표소에서는 버마어,
중국어, 몽어, 아이우미엔어, 크메르어, 한국어, 라오어, 파슈토어, 펀자브어,
타갈로그어, 태국어 및 베트남어로 표시된 샘플 투표용지를 제공합니다. 또한,
배정된 이중언어 선거 담당자와 그들이 구사하는 언어 정보가 포함된 전체
투표소 목록이 선거일 14일 전부터 온라인에 게시됩니다. 자세한 내용은
유권자 등록 사무소에 문의하십시오.

FP-LANGUAGE ASSISTANCE-ENG
LANGUAGE ASSISTANCE
Voters can get their ballots and other election materials in Spanish (Voting Rights Act of
1965). Polling places will have sample ballots available in all of the following languages:
Burmese, Chinese, Hmong, Iu Mien, Khmer, Korean, Lao, Pashto, Punjabi, Tagalog, Thai,
and Vietnamese. Additionally, a list of all polling places, including the assigned bilingual
Election Officers and the languages they speak, will be available online 14 days before the
election. For more information, contact the Registrar of Voters Office.

FP-UNDERSTANDING THE BALLOT-ENG
UNDERSTANDING THE GENERAL ELECTION BALLOT
WHY ARE THERE ONLY TWO CANDIDATES FOR SOME OFFICES?
California’s Top-Two Open Primary Act applies to voter-nominated offices. During the Primary
Election, all candidates appeared on the same ballot regardless of party preference. The two
candidates with the most votes advanced to the General Election, regardless of party preference.
WHY ARE BOTH CANDIDATES SOMETIMES FROM THE SAME PARTY?
Because the Top-Two system advances the two candidates receiving the most votes, both candidates
on the General Election ballot may have the same party preference, different party preferences, or no
party preference.
WHAT TYPES OF OFFICES ARE ON THIS BALLOT?
The General Election ballot includes voter-nominated and nonpartisan offices which all
registered voters regardless of party preference may vote on.
VOTER-NOMINATED OFFICES NONPARTISAN OFFICES
Examples include:
• Federal offices such as U.S. Senator or U.S.
Representative
• Governor and other statewide constitutional
offices
• State Senate
• State Assembly
• State Board of Equalization
Examples include:
• State Superintendent of Public Instruction
• County Supervisor
• Superior Court Judge
• Mayor
• City Council
WILL PARTY PREFERENCE APPEAR ON THE BALLOT?
VOTER-NOMINATED OFFICES NONPARTISAN OFFICES
The candidate’s party preference (or “None”)
appears on the ballot. A candidate’s party
preference does not mean the candidate is
nominated or endorsed by that political party.
Party preference does not appear on the ballot.
HOW DOES A CANDIDATE ADVANCE FROM THE
PRIMARY ELECTION TO THE GENERAL ELECTION?
VOTER-NOMINATED OFFICES NONPARTISAN OFFICES
The two candidates with the most votes in
the Primary Election advanced to the General
Election, regardless of party preference.
A candidate receiving a majority of votes (more
than 50%) in the Primary Election was elected.
If no candidate received a majority, the two
candidates with the most votes advanced to the
General Election.

FP-CANDIDATES AND MEASURES-ENG
CANDIDATE STATEMENT OF QUALIFICATIONS
A complete list of candidates for the offices you are eligible to vote on
based on your residence is provided on your sample ballot. Some of these
candidates have chosen to include a Candidate Statement of Qualifications
outlining their qualifications for the position. Candidates must pay for these
optional statements unless the governing body has chosen to cover the
cost. All Candidate Statements are printed exactly as submitted. Information
about candidates for statewide offices can be found in the State Voter
Information Guide.
The following state legislative candidates have accepted the voluntary
campaign expenditure limits and are eligible to submit a Candidate
Statement for printing in the County Voter Information Guide:
• Rhodesia Ransom
WRITE-IN CANDIDATES
On Election Day, the list of approved write-in candidates will be available at
all polling locations and on our website: www.sjcrov.org. Votes will only be
counted for officially recognized write-in candidates.
MEASURES
On your ballot and in this guide, you will see only the measures that apply to
the district in which you are registered to vote. Some measures may include
arguments in favor of or against them. These arguments represent solely
the opinions of their authors.
The measure text is printed exactly as submitted by the district. All arguments
are also printed exactly as submitted. Neither the measure text nor the
arguments have been edited or changed by the office producing this guide.
SJ COMPOSITE-012
12
FP-INSTRUCTIONS FOR VOTERS-ENG
INSTRUCTIONS FOR VOTING
How to mark your ballot:
Use blue or black ink ONLY.
You are not required to cast a vote in every contest. Contests left blank
will not affect the validity of your ballot.
To vote for a measure, fill in the box next to the word “Yes” or “No”.
To vote for a candidate, fill in the box next to the candidate’s name.
Write-in candidates:
To vote for a qualified write-in candidate, write the candidate’s name in
the blank space provided and fill in the box next to it.
Fixing mistakes on your ballot:
If you make a mistake, either draw a line through the unintended
choice and mark the box you want to vote on, or you may request a
new ballot.
A mistake in one contest does not affect the rest of the voted ballot.
Avoid an overvote:
Read each race carefully, do not select more candidates than the
number that is specified for that contest.

MEASURES SUBMITTED TO
THE VOTERS
STATE
Proposition 1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
HOUSING AFFORDABILITY
PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $11.25
billion in state general
obligation bonds for housing
affordability programs, including
multifamily rental housing,
mortgages for veterans,
supportive housing,
preservation of existing
affordable housing, and
downpayment assistance. Fiscal
Impact: Increased state cost of
$500 million to $600 million
annually for about 25 years to
repay the housing bond.
Supporters: US Vets; CA
Federation of Teachers; Self-
Help for the Elderly; Habitat for
Humanity CA; CA Alliance of
Child & Family Services
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 2
INCREASES STATE'S RAINY
DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Increases
California's Rainy Day Fund,
approved by voters in 2014, to
provide funding for education,
health care, public safety, and
other essential services during
economic downturns. Fiscal
Impact: State budget reserves
would be higher. Supporters:
CA Professional Firefighters; LA
Chamber of Commerce; Gavin
Newsom; Xavier Becerra;
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 3
PROVIDES PERMANENT
FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND
HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING
EXISTING TAX ON HIGH
INCOMES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Makes
permanent existing voter-
approved tax rates for
individuals earning over
$371,000 (adjusted annually for
inflation). Allocates tax revenues
to public education. Fiscal
Impact: Maintains $5 billion to
$15 billion of annual state
income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-
income earners permanent
instead of letting it expire in
2031. Supporters: California
Teachers Association; CA School
Nurses Organization; California
State PTA; Planned Parenthood
Affiliates of CA Opponents:
California Taxpayers Association;
Family Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
YES
NO
Proposition 4
REPEALS PROHIBITION
AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING
OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS.
LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
Repeals prohibition on state
and local governments
offering public funding of
candidate election
campaigns. Public funding
programs may not use funds
earmarked for education,
transportation, or public
safety. Fiscal Impact:
Ongoing costs to the state of
a few hundred thousand
dollars each year for the Fair
Political Practices Commission
to answer questions from
state and local governments
about public campaign
finance programs.
Supporters: League of
Women Voters of CA;
California Nurses Association;
Mental Health Advocacy;
Social Security Works;
Consumer Watchdog
Opponents: California
Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis
Taxpayers Assn; Family
Business Assn of California;
United Latinos Action
YES
NO

Proposition 5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION
PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE
OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Under current
law, voters elect replacement
candidates at the same time as
the recall election. This measure
instead fills recall vacancies by
subsequent special election or
appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net
fiscal effect unknown. In the
event of a recall, savings or costs
of millions of dollars to
administer the election
depending on the office
recalled. Supporters: None
submitted Opponents: None
submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM
FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS
OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES.
INITIATIVE STATUTE.
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds
to offer eligible buyers fixed-
rate mortgages for up to 17% of
purchase price of a newly
constructed home priced below
about $1.5 million. Borrowers
must be California residents,
occupy the home, meet income
limits, and pay at least 3% down.
Bonds repaid by mortgage
payments, not State. Fiscal
Impact: No direct state or local
costs. Supporters: United
Nurses Associations of
California; California Conference
of Carpenters; California State
Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents:
None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL
RESEARCH. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $8.4
billion in general obligation
bonds for immunology and
immunotherapy research, half to
a single University of California-
affiliated nonprofit medical
research institute, half to
research grants. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state cost of $500
million to $600 million annually
for about 20 years to repay the
research bond, with some or all
of the cost offset if the funded
research generates revenue.
Supporters: Michael J. Fox
Foundation; Alzheimer's Los
Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc;
American Nurses Assoc\CA
Opponents: Robert M Kaplan
Ph.D.
YES
NO
Proposition 39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM
VOTING UNLESS THEY
PRESENT GOVERNMENT-
ISSUED IDENTIFICATION.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Invalidates mail
ballots that do not have last four
digits of designated
government-issued
identification number written on
envelope. Prohibits in-person
voting without presenting
government-issued
identification. Fiscal Impact:
Costs of between tens of
millions of dollars and low
hundreds of millions of dollars
each year to implement new
voting requirements.
Supporters: The Transparency
Foundation; Latino American
Political Assn; Howard Jarvis
Taxpayers Assn; CA Women's
Leadership Assn Opponents:
ACLU California Action;
Common Cause; League of
Women Voters of California
YES
NO
Proposition 40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON
CERTAIN TAXPAYERS.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
Imposes 5% tax on certain
taxpayers with assets over $1
billion; revenue primarily for
health care. Exempts revenues
from constitutional
requirements for school funding
and spending limit. Fiscal
Impact: Temporary revenue
increase of tens of billions of
dollars spread over several years
from wealth tax on billionaires.
Possible ongoing decrease of
less than $1 billion per year in
income tax revenue from
billionaires. Supporters: US
Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU
United Healthcare Workers West
Opponents: California Primary
Care Association; California
School Boards Association;
California Taxpayers Association
YES
NO
Proposition 41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES
THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES
FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT.
REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW
STATE SPECIAL TAXES.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Nullifies state
taxes enacted after January 1,
2026 that exempt their revenues
from voter-approved state
spending limit. Requires pre-
election and recurring audits of
programs funded by new special
taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net
fiscal effect is unknown as it
depends on future decisions by
voters, the Legislature, and
other policymakers. Supporters:
CA Society of Certified Public
Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian
Chamber of Commerce;
California Taxpayers Association
(CalTax) Opponents: US Senator
Bernie Sanders; SEIU United
Healthcare Workers West
YES
NO

Proposition 42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE
PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES
AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE
STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Prohibits any
new state tax (1) imposed on the
ownership of personal property
(all things people own other
than real estate), or (2) that
applies retroactively based on
taxpayer's past activities.
Nullifies taxes enacted after
January 1, 2026 that conflict with
this measure. Fiscal Impact:
Possibility that tax revenues will
not go up as much in the future.
Supporters: CA Professional
Firefighters; State Building &
Construction Trades Council of
CA; AMVETS Department of CA
Opponents: US Senator Bernie
Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare
Workers West
YES
NO
Proposition 43
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO
RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
GOVERNMENT SERVICES.
LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Limits voters'
ability to pass voter-proposed
local special taxes by increasing
percentage of votes needed to
approve such ballot measures
from a majority (over 50%) to
two-thirds, beginning January 1,
2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility
that local government tax
revenues will not go up as much
in the future due to a higher
vote threshold for certain taxes.
Supporters: California
Taxpayers Association; Family
Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
Opponents: California
Professional Firefighters;
California Federation of
Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU
CA.
YES
NO
Proposition 44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY
HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90%
OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM
SERVICES. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Imposes penalties on
nonprofit Federally Qualified
Health Centers (community
clinics providing primary care to
medically underserved areas and
populations) that spend less
than 90% of revenue on
"program services" advancing
their charitable purpose,
including but not limited to
patient services. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state costs in the low
tens of millions of dollars per
year, covered by fees.
Supporters: None submitted
Opponents: American Academy
of Pediatrics CA; CA School
Nurses Org; CA Academy of
Family Physicians; CA Medical
Assoc.
YES
NO
Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL
REVIEW FOR CERTAIN
PROJECTS. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Amends California
Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) to expedite
environmental review for certain
projects (including most
housing, transportation, water,
and health projects) by setting
deadlines to complete
environmental review and
resolve lawsuits challenging
project approvals. Fiscal
Impact: Initial costs for state
and local governments, likely in
the high tens of millions of
dollars-potentially exceeding
$100 million-annually, partly
covered by fees. Uncertain,
potentially more significant
positive or negative longer-term
fiscal effects. Supporters:
California Children's Hospital
Association; California Water
Association; California Council
for Affordable Housing
Opponents: Coalition for Clean
Air; CA Environmental Voters;
Physicians for Social
Responsibility, LA; National
Wildlife Federation
YES
NO

MEASURES SUBMITTED TO

STATE
Proposition 1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
HOUSING AFFORDABILITY
PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $11.25
billion in state general
obligation bonds for housing
affordability programs, including
multifamily rental housing,
mortgages for veterans,
supportive housing,
preservation of existing
affordable housing, and
downpayment assistance. Fiscal
Impact: Increased state cost of
$500 million to $600 million
annually for about 25 years to
repay the housing bond.
Supporters: US Vets; CA
Federation of Teachers; Self-
Help for the Elderly; Habitat for
Humanity CA; CA Alliance of
Child & Family Services
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 2
INCREASES STATE'S RAINY
DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Increases
California's Rainy Day Fund,
approved by voters in 2014, to
provide funding for education,
health care, public safety, and
other essential services during
economic downturns. Fiscal
Impact: State budget reserves
would be higher. Supporters:
CA Professional Firefighters; LA
Chamber of Commerce; Gavin
Newsom; Xavier Becerra;
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 3
PROVIDES PERMANENT
FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND
HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING
EXISTING TAX ON HIGH
INCOMES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Makes
permanent existing voter-
approved tax rates for
individuals earning over
$371,000 (adjusted annually for
inflation). Allocates tax revenues
to public education. Fiscal
Impact: Maintains $5 billion to
$15 billion of annual state
income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-
income earners permanent
instead of letting it expire in
2031. Supporters: California
Teachers Association; CA School
Nurses Organization; California
State PTA; Planned Parenthood
Affiliates of CA Opponents:
California Taxpayers Association;
Family Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
YES
NO
Proposition 4
REPEALS PROHIBITION
AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING
OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS.
LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
Repeals prohibition on state
and local governments
offering public funding of
candidate election
campaigns. Public funding
programs may not use funds
earmarked for education,
transportation, or public
safety. Fiscal Impact:
Ongoing costs to the state of
a few hundred thousand
dollars each year for the Fair
Political Practices Commission
to answer questions from
state and local governments
about public campaign
finance programs.
Supporters: League of
Women Voters of CA;
California Nurses Association;
Mental Health Advocacy;
Social Security Works;
Consumer Watchdog
Opponents: California
Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis
Taxpayers Assn; Family
Business Assn of California;
United Latinos Action

Proposition 5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION
PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE
OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Under current

candidates at the same time as
the recall election. This measure
instead fills recall vacancies by
subsequent special election or
appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net
fiscal effect unknown. In the
event of a recall, savings or costs
of millions of dollars to
administer the election
depending on the office
recalled. Supporters: None
submitted Opponents: None
submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM
FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS
OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES.
INITIATIVE STATUTE.
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds
to offer eligible buyers fixed-
rate mortgages for up to 17% of
purchase price of a newly
constructed home priced below
about $1.5 million. Borrowers
must be California residents,
occupy the home, meet income
limits, and pay at least 3% down.
Bonds repaid by mortgage
payments, not State. Fiscal
Impact: No direct state or local
costs. Supporters: United
Nurses Associations of
California; California Conference
of Carpenters; California State
Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents:
None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL
RESEARCH. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $8.4
billion in general obligation
bonds for immunology and
immunotherapy research, half to
a single University of California-
affiliated nonprofit medical
research institute, half to
research grants. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state cost of $500
million to $600 million annually
for about 20 years to repay the
research bond, with some or all
of the cost offset if the funded
research generates revenue.
Supporters: Michael J. Fox
Foundation; Alzheimer's Los
Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc;
American Nurses Assoc\CA
Opponents: Robert M Kaplan
Ph.D.

Proposition 39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM

AMENDMENT. Invalidates mail
ballots that do not have last four
digits of designated
government-issued
identification number written on
envelope. Prohibits in-person
voting without presenting
government-issued
identification. Fiscal Impact:
Costs of between tens of
millions of dollars and low
hundreds of millions of dollars
each year to implement new
voting requirements.
Supporters: The Transparency

Women Voters of California

Proposition 40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON
CERTAIN TAXPAYERS.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
Imposes 5% tax on certain
taxpayers with assets over $1
billion; revenue primarily for
health care. Exempts revenues
from constitutional
requirements for school funding
and spending limit. Fiscal
Impact: Temporary revenue
increase of tens of billions of
dollars spread over several years
from wealth tax on billionaires.
Possible ongoing decrease of
less than $1 billion per year in
income tax revenue from
billionaires. Supporters: US
Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU
United Healthcare Workers West
Opponents: California Primary
Care Association; California
School Boards Association;
California Taxpayers Association
YES
NO
Proposition 41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES
THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES
FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT.
REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW
STATE SPECIAL TAXES.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Nullifies state
taxes enacted after January 1,
2026 that exempt their revenues
from voter-approved state
spending limit. Requires pre-
election and recurring audits of
programs funded by new special
taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net
fiscal effect is unknown as it
depends on future decisions by
voters, the Legislature, and
other policymakers. Supporters:
CA Society of Certified Public
Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian
Chamber of Commerce;
California Taxpayers Association
(CalTax) Opponents: US Senator
Bernie Sanders; SEIU United
Healthcare Workers West

Proposition 42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE
PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES
AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE
STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Prohibits any
new state tax (1) imposed on the
ownership of personal property
(all things people own other
than real estate), or (2) that
applies retroactively based on
taxpayer's past activities.
Nullifies taxes enacted after
January 1, 2026 that conflict with
this measure. Fiscal Impact:
Possibility that tax revenues will
not go up as much in the future.
Supporters: CA Professional
Firefighters; State Building &
Construction Trades Council of
CA; AMVETS Department of CA
Opponents: US Senator Bernie
Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare
Workers West
YES
NO
Proposition 43
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO
RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
GOVERNMENT SERVICES.
LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Limits voters'
ability to pass voter-proposed
local special taxes by increasing
percentage of votes needed to
approve such ballot measures
from a majority (over 50%) to
two-thirds, beginning January 1,
2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility
that local government tax
revenues will not go up as much
in the future due to a higher
vote threshold for certain taxes.
Supporters: California
Taxpayers Association; Family
Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
Opponents: California
Professional Firefighters;
California Federation of
Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU
CA.
YES
NO
Proposition 44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY
HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90%
OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM
SERVICES. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Imposes penalties on
nonprofit Federally Qualified
Health Centers (community
clinics providing primary care to
medically underserved areas and
populations) that spend less
than 90% of revenue on
"program services" advancing
their charitable purpose,
including but not limited to
patient services. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state costs in the low
tens of millions of dollars per
year, covered by fees.
Supporters: None submitted
Opponents: American Academy
of Pediatrics CA; CA School
Nurses Org; CA Academy of
Family Physicians; CA Medical
Assoc.
YES
NO
Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL
REVIEW FOR CERTAIN
PROJECTS. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Amends California
Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) to expedite
environmental review for certain
projects (including most
housing, transportation, water,
and health projects) by setting
deadlines to complete
environmental review and
resolve lawsuits challenging
project approvals. Fiscal
Impact: Initial costs for state
and local governments, likely in
the high tens of millions of
dollars-potentially exceeding
$100 million-annually, partly
covered by fees. Uncertain,
potentially more significant
positive or negative longer-term
fiscal effects. Supporters:
California Children's Hospital
Association; California Water
Association; California Council
for Affordable Housing
Opponents: Coalition for Clean
Air; CA Environmental Voters;
Physicians for Social
Responsibility, LA; National
Wildlife Federation

NO

CONSTITUTIONAL

provide funding for education,
health care, public safety, and
other essential services during
economic downturns. Fiscal
Impact: State budget reserves
would be higher. Supporters:

Opponents: None submitted

CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Makes
permanent existing voter-
approved tax rates for
individuals earning over
$371,000 (adjusted annually for
inflation). Allocates tax revenues
to public education. Fiscal
Impact: Maintains $5 billion to
$15 billion of annual state
income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-
income earners permanent
instead of letting it expire in
2031. Supporters: California

California Taxpayers Association;

California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce

Proposition 4
REPEALS PROHIBITION
AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING
OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS.
LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
Repeals prohibition on state
and local governments
offering public funding of
candidate election
campaigns. Public funding
programs may not use funds
earmarked for education,
transportation, or public
safety. Fiscal Impact:
Ongoing costs to the state of
a few hundred thousand
dollars each year for the Fair
Political Practices Commission
to answer questions from
state and local governments
about public campaign
finance programs.
Supporters: League of

Proposition 1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
HOUSING AFFORDABILITY
PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $11.25
billion in state general
obligation bonds for housing
affordability programs, including
multifamily rental housing,
mortgages for veterans,
supportive housing,
preservation of existing
affordable housing, and
downpayment assistance. Fiscal
Impact: Increased state cost of
$500 million to $600 million
annually for about 25 years to
repay the housing bond.
Supporters: US Vets; CA
Federation of Teachers; Self-
Help for the Elderly; Habitat for
Humanity CA; CA Alliance of
Child & Family Services
Opponents: None submitted

NO
Proposition 2
INCREASES STATE'S RAINY
DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Increases
California's Rainy Day Fund,
approved by voters in 2014, to
provide funding for education,
health care, public safety, and
other essential services during
economic downturns. Fiscal
Impact: State budget reserves
would be higher. Supporters:
CA Professional Firefighters; LA
Chamber of Commerce; Gavin
Newsom; Xavier Becerra;
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 3
PROVIDES PERMANENT
FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND
HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING
EXISTING TAX ON HIGH
INCOMES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Makes
permanent existing voter-
approved tax rates for
individuals earning over
$371,000 (adjusted annually for
inflation). Allocates tax revenues
to public education. Fiscal
Impact: Maintains $5 billion to
$15 billion of annual state
income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-
income earners permanent
instead of letting it expire in
2031. Supporters: California
Teachers Association; CA School
Nurses Organization; California
State PTA; Planned Parenthood
Affiliates of CA Opponents:
California Taxpayers Association;
Family Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce

Repeals prohibition on state
and local governments
offering public funding of
candidate election
campaigns. Public funding
programs may not use funds
earmarked for education,

Ongoing costs to the state of

CREATES LOAN PROGRAM
FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS

Authorizes $25 billion in bonds
to offer eligible buyers fixed-
rate mortgages for up to 17% of
purchase price of a newly
constructed home priced below
about $1.5 million. Borrowers
must be California residents,
occupy the home, meet income
limits, and pay at least 3% down.
Bonds repaid by mortgage
payments, not State. Fiscal

costs. Supporters: United

STATUTE. Authorizes $8.4
billion in general obligation
bonds for immunology and
immunotherapy research, half to
a single University of California-
affiliated nonprofit medical
research institute, half to
research grants. Fiscal Impact:

for about 20 years to repay the

hundreds of millions of dollars

Proposition 40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON
CERTAIN TAXPAYERS.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
Imposes 5% tax on certain
taxpayers with assets over $1
billion; revenue primarily for
health care. Exempts revenues
from constitutional
requirements for school funding
and spending limit. Fiscal
Impact: Temporary revenue
increase of tens of billions of
dollars spread over several years
from wealth tax on billionaires.
Possible ongoing decrease of
less than $1 billion per year in
income tax revenue from
billionaires. Supporters: US
Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU
United Healthcare Workers West
Opponents: California Primary
Care Association; California
School Boards Association;
California Taxpayers Association

Proposition 41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES
THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES
FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT.
REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW
STATE SPECIAL TAXES.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Nullifies state
taxes enacted after January 1,
2026 that exempt their revenues
from voter-approved state
spending limit. Requires pre-
election and recurring audits of
programs funded by new special
taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net
fiscal effect is unknown as it
depends on future decisions by
voters, the Legislature, and
other policymakers. Supporters:
CA Society of Certified Public
Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian
Chamber of Commerce;
California Taxpayers Association
(CalTax) Opponents: US Senator
Bernie Sanders; SEIU United
Healthcare Workers West

Proposition 42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE
PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES
AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE
STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Prohibits any
new state tax (1) imposed on the
ownership of personal property
(all things people own other
than real estate), or (2) that
applies retroactively based on
taxpayer's past activities.
Nullifies taxes enacted after
January 1, 2026 that conflict with
this measure. Fiscal Impact:
Possibility that tax revenues will
not go up as much in the future.
Supporters: CA Professional
Firefighters; State Building &
Construction Trades Council of
CA; AMVETS Department of CA
Opponents: US Senator Bernie
Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare
Workers West
YES
NO
Proposition 43
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO
RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
GOVERNMENT SERVICES.
LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Limits voters'
ability to pass voter-proposed
local special taxes by increasing
percentage of votes needed to
approve such ballot measures
from a majority (over 50%) to
two-thirds, beginning January 1,
2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility
that local government tax
revenues will not go up as much
in the future due to a higher
vote threshold for certain taxes.
Supporters: California
Taxpayers Association; Family
Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
Opponents: California
Professional Firefighters;
California Federation of
Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU
CA.
YES
NO
Proposition 44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY
HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90%
OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM
SERVICES. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Imposes penalties on
nonprofit Federally Qualified
Health Centers (community
clinics providing primary care to
medically underserved areas and
populations) that spend less
than 90% of revenue on
"program services" advancing
their charitable purpose,
including but not limited to
patient services. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state costs in the low
tens of millions of dollars per
year, covered by fees.
Supporters: None submitted
Opponents: American Academy
of Pediatrics CA; CA School
Nurses Org; CA Academy of
Family Physicians; CA Medical
Assoc.
YES
NO
Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL
REVIEW FOR CERTAIN
PROJECTS. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Amends California
Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) to expedite
environmental review for certain
projects (including most
housing, transportation, water,
and health projects) by setting
deadlines to complete
environmental review and
resolve lawsuits challenging
project approvals. Fiscal
Impact: Initial costs for state
and local governments, likely in
the high tens of millions of
dollars-potentially exceeding
$100 million-annually, partly
covered by fees. Uncertain,
potentially more significant
positive or negative longer-term
fiscal effects. Supporters:
California Children's Hospital
Association; California Water
Association; California Council
for Affordable Housing
Opponents: Coalition for Clean
Air; CA Environmental Voters;
Physicians for Social
Responsibility, LA; National
Wildlife Federation
YES
NO

MEASURES SUBMITTED TO
THE VOTERS
STATE
Proposition 1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
HOUSING AFFORDABILITY
PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $11.25
billion in state general
obligation bonds for housing
affordability programs, including
multifamily rental housing,
mortgages for veterans,
supportive housing,
preservation of existing
affordable housing, and
downpayment assistance. Fiscal
Impact: Increased state cost of
$500 million to $600 million
annually for about 25 years to
repay the housing bond.
Supporters: US Vets; CA
Federation of Teachers; Self-
Help for the Elderly; Habitat for
Humanity CA; CA Alliance of
Child & Family Services
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 2
INCREASES STATE'S RAINY
DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Increases
California's Rainy Day Fund,
approved by voters in 2014, to
provide funding for education,
health care, public safety, and
other essential services during
economic downturns. Fiscal
Impact: State budget reserves
would be higher. Supporters:
CA Professional Firefighters; LA
Chamber of Commerce; Gavin
Newsom; Xavier Becerra;
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 3
PROVIDES PERMANENT
FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND
HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING
EXISTING TAX ON HIGH
INCOMES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Makes
permanent existing voter-
approved tax rates for
individuals earning over
$371,000 (adjusted annually for
inflation). Allocates tax revenues
to public education. Fiscal
Impact: Maintains $5 billion to
$15 billion of annual state
income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-
income earners permanent
instead of letting it expire in
2031. Supporters: California
Teachers Association; CA School
Nurses Organization; California
State PTA; Planned Parenthood
Affiliates of CA Opponents:
California Taxpayers Association;
Family Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
YES
NO
Proposition 4
REPEALS PROHIBITION
AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING
OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS.
LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
Repeals prohibition on state
and local governments
offering public funding of
candidate election
campaigns. Public funding
programs may not use funds
earmarked for education,
transportation, or public
safety. Fiscal Impact:
Ongoing costs to the state of
a few hundred thousand
dollars each year for the Fair
Political Practices Commission
to answer questions from
state and local governments
about public campaign
finance programs.
Supporters: League of
Women Voters of CA;
California Nurses Association;
Mental Health Advocacy;
Social Security Works;
Consumer Watchdog
Opponents: California
Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis
Taxpayers Assn; Family
Business Assn of California;
United Latinos Action
YES
NO

Proposition 5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION
PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE
OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Under current
law, voters elect replacement
candidates at the same time as
the recall election. This measure
instead fills recall vacancies by
subsequent special election or
appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net
fiscal effect unknown. In the
event of a recall, savings or costs
of millions of dollars to
administer the election
depending on the office
recalled. Supporters: None
submitted Opponents: None
submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM
FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS
OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES.
INITIATIVE STATUTE.
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds
to offer eligible buyers fixed-
rate mortgages for up to 17% of
purchase price of a newly
constructed home priced below
about $1.5 million. Borrowers
must be California residents,
occupy the home, meet income
limits, and pay at least 3% down.
Bonds repaid by mortgage
payments, not State. Fiscal
Impact: No direct state or local
costs. Supporters: United
Nurses Associations of
California; California Conference
of Carpenters; California State
Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents:
None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL
RESEARCH. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $8.4
billion in general obligation
bonds for immunology and
immunotherapy research, half to
a single University of California-
affiliated nonprofit medical
research institute, half to
research grants. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state cost of $500
million to $600 million annually
for about 20 years to repay the
research bond, with some or all
of the cost offset if the funded
research generates revenue.
Supporters: Michael J. Fox
Foundation; Alzheimer's Los
Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc;
American Nurses Assoc\CA
Opponents: Robert M Kaplan
Ph.D.
YES
NO
Proposition 39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM
VOTING UNLESS THEY
PRESENT GOVERNMENT-
ISSUED IDENTIFICATION.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Invalidates mail
ballots that do not have last four
digits of designated
government-issued
identification number written on
envelope. Prohibits in-person
voting without presenting
government-issued
identification. Fiscal Impact:
Costs of between tens of
millions of dollars and low
hundreds of millions of dollars
each year to implement new
voting requirements.
Supporters: The Transparency
Foundation; Latino American
Political Assn; Howard Jarvis
Taxpayers Assn; CA Women's
Leadership Assn Opponents:
ACLU California Action;
Common Cause; League of
Women Voters of California
YES
NO
Proposition 40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON
CERTAIN TAXPAYERS.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
Imposes 5% tax on certain
taxpayers with assets over $1
billion; revenue primarily for
health care. Exempts revenues
from constitutional
requirements for school funding
and spending limit. Fiscal
Impact: Temporary revenue
increase of tens of billions of
dollars spread over several years
from wealth tax on billionaires.
Possible ongoing decrease of
less than $1 billion per year in
income tax revenue from
billionaires. Supporters: US
Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU
United Healthcare Workers West
Opponents: California Primary
Care Association; California
School Boards Association;
California Taxpayers Association
YES
NO
Proposition 41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES
THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES
FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT.
REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW
STATE SPECIAL TAXES.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Nullifies state
taxes enacted after January 1,
2026 that exempt their revenues
from voter-approved state
spending limit. Requires pre-
election and recurring audits of
programs funded by new special
taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net
fiscal effect is unknown as it
depends on future decisions by
voters, the Legislature, and
other policymakers. Supporters:
CA Society of Certified Public
Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian
Chamber of Commerce;
California Taxpayers Association
(CalTax) Opponents: US Senator
Bernie Sanders; SEIU United
Healthcare Workers West
YES
NO

Proposition 42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE
PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES
AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE
STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Prohibits any
new state tax (1) imposed on the
ownership of personal property
(all things people own other
than real estate), or (2) that
applies retroactively based on
taxpayer's past activities.
Nullifies taxes enacted after
January 1, 2026 that conflict with
this measure. Fiscal Impact:
Possibility that tax revenues will
not go up as much in the future.
Supporters: CA Professional
Firefighters; State Building &
Construction Trades Council of
CA; AMVETS Department of CA
Opponents: US Senator Bernie
Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare
Workers West
YES
NO
Proposition 43
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO
RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
GOVERNMENT SERVICES.
LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Limits voters'
ability to pass voter-proposed
local special taxes by increasing
percentage of votes needed to
approve such ballot measures
from a majority (over 50%) to
two-thirds, beginning January 1,
2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility
that local government tax
revenues will not go up as much
in the future due to a higher
vote threshold for certain taxes.
Supporters: California
Taxpayers Association; Family
Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
Opponents: California
Professional Firefighters;
California Federation of
Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU
CA.
YES
NO
Proposition 44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY
HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90%
OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM
SERVICES. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Imposes penalties on
nonprofit Federally Qualified
Health Centers (community
clinics providing primary care to
medically underserved areas and
populations) that spend less
than 90% of revenue on
"program services" advancing
their charitable purpose,
including but not limited to
patient services. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state costs in the low
tens of millions of dollars per
year, covered by fees.
Supporters: None submitted
Opponents: American Academy
of Pediatrics CA; CA School
Nurses Org; CA Academy of
Family Physicians; CA Medical
Assoc.
YES
NO
Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL
REVIEW FOR CERTAIN
PROJECTS. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Amends California
Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) to expedite
environmental review for certain
projects (including most
housing, transportation, water,
and health projects) by setting
deadlines to complete
environmental review and
resolve lawsuits challenging
project approvals. Fiscal
Impact: Initial costs for state
and local governments, likely in
the high tens of millions of
dollars-potentially exceeding
$100 million-annually, partly
covered by fees. Uncertain,
potentially more significant
positive or negative longer-term
fiscal effects. Supporters:
California Children's Hospital
Association; California Water
Association; California Council
for Affordable Housing
Opponents: Coalition for Clean
Air; CA Environmental Voters;
Physicians for Social
Responsibility, LA; National
Wildlife Federation
YES
NO

Proposition 1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
HOUSING AFFORDABILITY
PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $11.25
billion in state general
obligation bonds for housing
affordability programs, including
multifamily rental housing,
mortgages for veterans,
supportive housing,
preservation of existing
affordable housing, and
downpayment assistance. Fiscal
Impact: Increased state cost of
$500 million to $600 million
annually for about 25 years to
repay the housing bond.

Opponents: None submitted

provide funding for education,

economic downturns. Fiscal

Opponents: None submitted

$371,000 (adjusted annually for
inflation). Allocates tax revenues
to public education. Fiscal
Impact: Maintains $5 billion to
$15 billion of annual state

Proposition 42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE
PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES
AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE
STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Prohibits any
new state tax (1) imposed on the

January 1, 2026 that conflict with
this measure. Fiscal Impact:
Possibility that tax revenues will
not go up as much in the future.

Proposition 43
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO
RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
GOVERNMENT SERVICES.
LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Limits voters'
ability to pass voter-proposed
local special taxes by increasing
percentage of votes needed to
approve such ballot measures
from a majority (over 50%) to
two-thirds, beginning January 1,
2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility
that local government tax
revenues will not go up as much
in the future due to a higher
vote threshold for certain taxes.
Supporters: California

REQUIRES COMMUNITY

STATUTE. Imposes penalties on
nonprofit Federally Qualified
Health Centers (community
clinics providing primary care to
medically underserved areas and
populations) that spend less
than 90% of revenue on
"program services" advancing
their charitable purpose,
including but not limited to
patient services. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state costs in the low

Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL

STATUTE. Amends California
Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) to expedite
environmental review for certain
projects (including most
housing, transportation, water,
and health projects) by setting
deadlines to complete
environmental review and
resolve lawsuits challenging
project approvals. Fiscal
Impact: Initial costs for state
and local governments, likely in
the high tens of millions of

potentially more significant

Opponents: Coalition for Clean

MEASURES SUBMITTED TO
THE VOTERS
STATE
Proposition 1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
HOUSING AFFORDABILITY
PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $11.25
billion in state general
obligation bonds for housing
affordability programs, including
multifamily rental housing,
mortgages for veterans,
supportive housing,
preservation of existing
affordable housing, and
downpayment assistance. Fiscal
Impact: Increased state cost of
$500 million to $600 million
annually for about 25 years to
repay the housing bond.
Supporters: US Vets; CA
Federation of Teachers; Self-
Help for the Elderly; Habitat for
Humanity CA; CA Alliance of
Child & Family Services
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 2
INCREASES STATE'S RAINY
DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Increases
California's Rainy Day Fund,
approved by voters in 2014, to
provide funding for education,
health care, public safety, and
other essential services during
economic downturns. Fiscal
Impact: State budget reserves
would be higher. Supporters:
CA Professional Firefighters; LA
Chamber of Commerce; Gavin
Newsom; Xavier Becerra;
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 3
PROVIDES PERMANENT
FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND
HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING
EXISTING TAX ON HIGH
INCOMES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Makes
permanent existing voter-
approved tax rates for
individuals earning over
$371,000 (adjusted annually for
inflation). Allocates tax revenues
to public education. Fiscal
Impact: Maintains $5 billion to
$15 billion of annual state
income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-
income earners permanent
instead of letting it expire in
2031. Supporters: California
Teachers Association; CA School
Nurses Organization; California
State PTA; Planned Parenthood
Affiliates of CA Opponents:
California Taxpayers Association;
Family Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
YES
NO
Proposition 4
REPEALS PROHIBITION
AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING
OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS.
LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
Repeals prohibition on state
and local governments
offering public funding of
candidate election
campaigns. Public funding
programs may not use funds
earmarked for education,
transportation, or public
safety. Fiscal Impact:
Ongoing costs to the state of
a few hundred thousand
dollars each year for the Fair
Political Practices Commission
to answer questions from
state and local governments
about public campaign
finance programs.
Supporters: League of
Women Voters of CA;
California Nurses Association;
Mental Health Advocacy;
Social Security Works;
Consumer Watchdog
Opponents: California
Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis
Taxpayers Assn; Family
Business Assn of California;
United Latinos Action
YES
NO

Proposition 5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION
PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE
OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Under current
law, voters elect replacement
candidates at the same time as
the recall election. This measure
instead fills recall vacancies by
subsequent special election or
appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net
fiscal effect unknown. In the
event of a recall, savings or costs
of millions of dollars to
administer the election
depending on the office
recalled. Supporters: None
submitted Opponents: None
submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM
FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS
OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES.
INITIATIVE STATUTE.
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds
to offer eligible buyers fixed-
rate mortgages for up to 17% of
purchase price of a newly
constructed home priced below
about $1.5 million. Borrowers
must be California residents,
occupy the home, meet income
limits, and pay at least 3% down.
Bonds repaid by mortgage
payments, not State. Fiscal
Impact: No direct state or local
costs. Supporters: United
Nurses Associations of
California; California Conference
of Carpenters; California State
Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents:
None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL
RESEARCH. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $8.4
billion in general obligation
bonds for immunology and
immunotherapy research, half to
a single University of California-
affiliated nonprofit medical
research institute, half to
research grants. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state cost of $500
million to $600 million annually
for about 20 years to repay the
research bond, with some or all
of the cost offset if the funded
research generates revenue.
Supporters: Michael J. Fox
Foundation; Alzheimer's Los
Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc;
American Nurses Assoc\CA
Opponents: Robert M Kaplan
Ph.D.
YES
NO
Proposition 39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM
VOTING UNLESS THEY
PRESENT GOVERNMENT-
ISSUED IDENTIFICATION.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Invalidates mail
ballots that do not have last four
digits of designated
government-issued
identification number written on
envelope. Prohibits in-person
voting without presenting
government-issued
identification. Fiscal Impact:
Costs of between tens of
millions of dollars and low
hundreds of millions of dollars
each year to implement new
voting requirements.
Supporters: The Transparency
Foundation; Latino American
Political Assn; Howard Jarvis
Taxpayers Assn; CA Women's
Leadership Assn Opponents:
ACLU California Action;
Common Cause; League of
Women Voters of California
YES
NO
Proposition 40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON
CERTAIN TAXPAYERS.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
Imposes 5% tax on certain
taxpayers with assets over $1
billion; revenue primarily for
health care. Exempts revenues
from constitutional
requirements for school funding
and spending limit. Fiscal
Impact: Temporary revenue
increase of tens of billions of
dollars spread over several years
from wealth tax on billionaires.
Possible ongoing decrease of
less than $1 billion per year in
income tax revenue from
billionaires. Supporters: US
Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU
United Healthcare Workers West
Opponents: California Primary
Care Association; California
School Boards Association;
California Taxpayers Association
YES
NO
Proposition 41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES
THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES
FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT.
REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW
STATE SPECIAL TAXES.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Nullifies state
taxes enacted after January 1,
2026 that exempt their revenues
from voter-approved state
spending limit. Requires pre-
election and recurring audits of
programs funded by new special
taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net
fiscal effect is unknown as it
depends on future decisions by
voters, the Legislature, and
other policymakers. Supporters:
CA Society of Certified Public
Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian
Chamber of Commerce;
California Taxpayers Association
(CalTax) Opponents: US Senator
Bernie Sanders; SEIU United
Healthcare Workers West
YES
NO

Proposition 42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE
PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES
AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE
STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Prohibits any
new state tax (1) imposed on the
ownership of personal property
(all things people own other
than real estate), or (2) that
applies retroactively based on
taxpayer's past activities.
Nullifies taxes enacted after
January 1, 2026 that conflict with
this measure. Fiscal Impact:
Possibility that tax revenues will
not go up as much in the future.
Supporters: CA Professional
Firefighters; State Building &
Construction Trades Council of
CA; AMVETS Department of CA
Opponents: US Senator Bernie
Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare
Workers West
YES
NO
Proposition 43
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO
RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
GOVERNMENT SERVICES.
LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Limits voters'
ability to pass voter-proposed
local special taxes by increasing
percentage of votes needed to
approve such ballot measures
from a majority (over 50%) to
two-thirds, beginning January 1,
2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility
that local government tax
revenues will not go up as much
in the future due to a higher
vote threshold for certain taxes.
Supporters: California
Taxpayers Association; Family
Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
Opponents: California
Professional Firefighters;
California Federation of
Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU
CA.
YES
NO
Proposition 44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY
HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90%
OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM
SERVICES. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Imposes penalties on
nonprofit Federally Qualified
Health Centers (community
clinics providing primary care to
medically underserved areas and
populations) that spend less
than 90% of revenue on
"program services" advancing
their charitable purpose,
including but not limited to
patient services. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state costs in the low
tens of millions of dollars per
year, covered by fees.
Supporters: None submitted
Opponents: American Academy
of Pediatrics CA; CA School
Nurses Org; CA Academy of
Family Physicians; CA Medical
Assoc.
YES
NO
Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL
REVIEW FOR CERTAIN
PROJECTS. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Amends California
Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) to expedite
environmental review for certain
projects (including most
housing, transportation, water,
and health projects) by setting
deadlines to complete
environmental review and
resolve lawsuits challenging
project approvals. Fiscal
Impact: Initial costs for state
and local governments, likely in
the high tens of millions of
dollars-potentially exceeding
$100 million-annually, partly
covered by fees. Uncertain,
potentially more significant
positive or negative longer-term
fiscal effects. Supporters:
California Children's Hospital
Association; California Water
Association; California Council
for Affordable Housing
Opponents: Coalition for Clean
Air; CA Environmental Voters;
Physicians for Social
Responsibility, LA; National
Wildlife Federation
YES
NO
SCHOOL
Measure V
Lincoln Unified School District
Facilities and Safety Measure.
To improve the quality of
education; make safety/security
improvements; provide

$79,000,000 of bonds be

while bonds are outstanding,
with citizens' oversight, audits,
no money for salaries and
funding only for LUSD schools?

Proposition 42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE

AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE
STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Prohibits any
new state tax (1) imposed on the
ownership of personal property
(all things people own other

applies retroactively based on
taxpayer's past activities.

January 1, 2026 that conflict with
this measure. Fiscal Impact:
Possibility that tax revenues will
not go up as much in the future.

Proposition 43
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO
RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
GOVERNMENT SERVICES.
LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Limits voters'
ability to pass voter-proposed
local special taxes by increasing
percentage of votes needed to
approve such ballot measures
from a majority (over 50%) to
two-thirds, beginning January 1,
2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility
that local government tax
revenues will not go up as much
in the future due to a higher
vote threshold for certain taxes.
Supporters: California
Taxpayers Association; Family
Business Association of

Chambers of Commerce
Opponents: California

Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU
CA.

REQUIRES COMMUNITY

OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM
SERVICES. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Imposes penalties on
nonprofit Federally Qualified
Health Centers (community
clinics providing primary care to
medically underserved areas and
populations) that spend less
than 90% of revenue on
"program services" advancing
their charitable purpose,
including but not limited to
patient services. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state costs in the low
tens of millions of dollars per
year, covered by fees.
Supporters: None submitted
Opponents: American Academy

Nurses Org; CA Academy of

Assoc.

Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL
REVIEW FOR CERTAIN
PROJECTS. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Amends California
Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) to expedite
environmental review for certain
projects (including most
housing, transportation, water,
and health projects) by setting
deadlines to complete
environmental review and
resolve lawsuits challenging
project approvals. Fiscal
Impact: Initial costs for state
and local governments, likely in
the high tens of millions of
dollars-potentially exceeding
$100 million-annually, partly
covered by fees. Uncertain,
potentially more significant
positive or negative longer-term
fiscal effects. Supporters:

for Affordable Housing
Opponents: Coalition for Clean
Air; CA Environmental Voters;

Responsibility, LA; National
Wildlife Federation

MEASURES SUBMITTED TO
THE VOTERS
STATE
Proposition 1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
HOUSING AFFORDABILITY
PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $11.25
billion in state general
obligation bonds for housing
affordability programs, including
multifamily rental housing,
mortgages for veterans,
supportive housing,
preservation of existing
affordable housing, and
downpayment assistance. Fiscal
Impact: Increased state cost of
$500 million to $600 million
annually for about 25 years to
repay the housing bond.
Supporters: US Vets; CA
Federation of Teachers; Self-
Help for the Elderly; Habitat for
Humanity CA; CA Alliance of
Child & Family Services
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 2
INCREASES STATE'S RAINY
DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Increases
California's Rainy Day Fund,
approved by voters in 2014, to
provide funding for education,
health care, public safety, and
other essential services during
economic downturns. Fiscal
Impact: State budget reserves
would be higher. Supporters:
CA Professional Firefighters; LA
Chamber of Commerce; Gavin
Newsom; Xavier Becerra;
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel
Opponents: None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 3
PROVIDES PERMANENT
FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND
HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING
EXISTING TAX ON HIGH
INCOMES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Makes
permanent existing voter-
approved tax rates for
individuals earning over
$371,000 (adjusted annually for
inflation). Allocates tax revenues
to public education. Fiscal
Impact: Maintains $5 billion to
$15 billion of annual state
income tax revenue by making a
temporary tax increase on high-
income earners permanent
instead of letting it expire in
2031. Supporters: California
Teachers Association; CA School
Nurses Organization; California
State PTA; Planned Parenthood
Affiliates of CA Opponents:
California Taxpayers Association;
Family Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
YES
NO
Proposition 4
REPEALS PROHIBITION
AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING
OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS.
LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
Repeals prohibition on state
and local governments
offering public funding of
candidate election
campaigns. Public funding
programs may not use funds
earmarked for education,
transportation, or public
safety. Fiscal Impact:
Ongoing costs to the state of
a few hundred thousand
dollars each year for the Fair
Political Practices Commission
to answer questions from
state and local governments
about public campaign
finance programs.
Supporters: League of
Women Voters of CA;
California Nurses Association;
Mental Health Advocacy;
Social Security Works;
Consumer Watchdog
Opponents: California
Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis
Taxpayers Assn; Family
Business Assn of California;
United Latinos Action
YES
NO

Proposition 5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION
PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE
OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Under current
law, voters elect replacement
candidates at the same time as
the recall election. This measure
instead fills recall vacancies by
subsequent special election or
appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net
fiscal effect unknown. In the
event of a recall, savings or costs
of millions of dollars to
administer the election
depending on the office
recalled. Supporters: None
submitted Opponents: None
submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM
FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS
OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES.
INITIATIVE STATUTE.
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds
to offer eligible buyers fixed-
rate mortgages for up to 17% of
purchase price of a newly
constructed home priced below
about $1.5 million. Borrowers
must be California residents,
occupy the home, meet income
limits, and pay at least 3% down.
Bonds repaid by mortgage
payments, not State. Fiscal
Impact: No direct state or local
costs. Supporters: United
Nurses Associations of
California; California Conference
of Carpenters; California State
Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents:
None submitted
YES
NO
Proposition 38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR
IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL
RESEARCH. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Authorizes $8.4
billion in general obligation
bonds for immunology and
immunotherapy research, half to
a single University of California-
affiliated nonprofit medical
research institute, half to
research grants. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state cost of $500
million to $600 million annually
for about 20 years to repay the
research bond, with some or all
of the cost offset if the funded
research generates revenue.
Supporters: Michael J. Fox
Foundation; Alzheimer's Los
Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc;
American Nurses Assoc\CA
Opponents: Robert M Kaplan
Ph.D.
YES
NO
Proposition 39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM
VOTING UNLESS THEY
PRESENT GOVERNMENT-
ISSUED IDENTIFICATION.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Invalidates mail
ballots that do not have last four
digits of designated
government-issued
identification number written on
envelope. Prohibits in-person
voting without presenting
government-issued
identification. Fiscal Impact:
Costs of between tens of
millions of dollars and low
hundreds of millions of dollars
each year to implement new
voting requirements.
Supporters: The Transparency
Foundation; Latino American
Political Assn; Howard Jarvis
Taxpayers Assn; CA Women's
Leadership Assn Opponents:
ACLU California Action;
Common Cause; League of
Women Voters of California
YES
NO
Proposition 40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON
CERTAIN TAXPAYERS.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
Imposes 5% tax on certain
taxpayers with assets over $1
billion; revenue primarily for
health care. Exempts revenues
from constitutional
requirements for school funding
and spending limit. Fiscal
Impact: Temporary revenue
increase of tens of billions of
dollars spread over several years
from wealth tax on billionaires.
Possible ongoing decrease of
less than $1 billion per year in
income tax revenue from
billionaires. Supporters: US
Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU
United Healthcare Workers West
Opponents: California Primary
Care Association; California
School Boards Association;
California Taxpayers Association
YES
NO
Proposition 41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES
THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES
FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT.
REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW
STATE SPECIAL TAXES.
INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Nullifies state
taxes enacted after January 1,
2026 that exempt their revenues
from voter-approved state
spending limit. Requires pre-
election and recurring audits of
programs funded by new special
taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net
fiscal effect is unknown as it
depends on future decisions by
voters, the Legislature, and
other policymakers. Supporters:
CA Society of Certified Public
Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian
Chamber of Commerce;
California Taxpayers Association
(CalTax) Opponents: US Senator
Bernie Sanders; SEIU United
Healthcare Workers West
YES
NO

Proposition 42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE
PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES
AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE
STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Prohibits any
new state tax (1) imposed on the
ownership of personal property
(all things people own other
than real estate), or (2) that
applies retroactively based on
taxpayer's past activities.
Nullifies taxes enacted after
January 1, 2026 that conflict with
this measure. Fiscal Impact:
Possibility that tax revenues will
not go up as much in the future.
Supporters: CA Professional
Firefighters; State Building &
Construction Trades Council of
CA; AMVETS Department of CA
Opponents: US Senator Bernie
Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare
Workers West
YES
NO
Proposition 43
LIMITS VOTERS' ABILITY TO
RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
GOVERNMENT SERVICES.
LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Limits voters'
ability to pass voter-proposed
local special taxes by increasing
percentage of votes needed to
approve such ballot measures
from a majority (over 50%) to
two-thirds, beginning January 1,
2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility
that local government tax
revenues will not go up as much
in the future due to a higher
vote threshold for certain taxes.
Supporters: California
Taxpayers Association; Family
Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
Opponents: California
Professional Firefighters;
California Federation of
Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU
CA.
YES
NO
Proposition 44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY
HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90%
OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM
SERVICES. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Imposes penalties on
nonprofit Federally Qualified
Health Centers (community
clinics providing primary care to
medically underserved areas and
populations) that spend less
than 90% of revenue on
"program services" advancing
their charitable purpose,
including but not limited to
patient services. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state costs in the low
tens of millions of dollars per
year, covered by fees.
Supporters: None submitted
Opponents: American Academy
of Pediatrics CA; CA School
Nurses Org; CA Academy of
Family Physicians; CA Medical
Assoc.
YES
NO
Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL
REVIEW FOR CERTAIN
PROJECTS. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Amends California
Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) to expedite
environmental review for certain
projects (including most
housing, transportation, water,
and health projects) by setting
deadlines to complete
environmental review and
resolve lawsuits challenging
project approvals. Fiscal
Impact: Initial costs for state
and local governments, likely in
the high tens of millions of
dollars-potentially exceeding
$100 million-annually, partly
covered by fees. Uncertain,
potentially more significant
positive or negative longer-term
fiscal effects. Supporters:
California Children's Hospital
Association; California Water
Association; California Council
for Affordable Housing
Opponents: Coalition for Clean
Air; CA Environmental Voters;
Physicians for Social
Responsibility, LA; National
Wildlife Federation
YES
NO

RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL
GOVERNMENT SERVICES.
LEGISLATIVE
CONSTITUTIONAL
AMENDMENT. Limits voters'
ability to pass voter-proposed
local special taxes by increasing
percentage of votes needed to
approve such ballot measures
from a majority (over 50%) to
two-thirds, beginning January 1,
2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility
that local government tax
revenues will not go up as much
in the future due to a higher
vote threshold for certain taxes.
Supporters: California
Taxpayers Association; Family
Business Association of
California; California Hispanic
Chambers of Commerce
Opponents: California
Professional Firefighters;
California Federation of
Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU
CA.
YES
NO
Proposition 44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY
HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90%
OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM
SERVICES. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Imposes penalties on
nonprofit Federally Qualified
Health Centers (community
clinics providing primary care to
medically underserved areas and
populations) that spend less
than 90% of revenue on
"program services" advancing
their charitable purpose,
including but not limited to
patient services. Fiscal Impact:
Increased state costs in the low
tens of millions of dollars per
year, covered by fees.
Supporters: None submitted
Opponents: American Academy
of Pediatrics CA; CA School
Nurses Org; CA Academy of
Family Physicians; CA Medical
Assoc.
YES
NO
Proposition 45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL
REVIEW FOR CERTAIN
PROJECTS. INITIATIVE
STATUTE. Amends California
Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) to expedite
environmental review for certain
projects (including most
housing, transportation, water,
and health projects) by setting
deadlines to complete
environmental review and
resolve lawsuits challenging
project approvals. Fiscal
Impact: Initial costs for state
and local governments, likely in
the high tens of millions of
dollars-potentially exceeding
$100 million-annually, partly
covered by fees. Uncertain,
potentially more significant
positive or negative longer-term
fiscal effects. Supporters:
California Children's Hospital
Association; California Water
Association; California Council
for Affordable Housing
Opponents: Coalition for Clean
Air; CA Environmental Voters;
Physicians for Social
Responsibility, LA; National
Wildlife Federation
YES
NO
